demonstrations.title: How much does setting a hint change the answers?
demonstrations.question: A rule answers yes when its evidence score plus the hint's points is zero or higher. What does setting the hint present change?

symbols_list.meaning: the answer: 1 for yes, 0 for no
the hint: 1 present, 0 absent
we set the hint ourselves to h
difference between the two proportions of yes, for these cases

demonstrations.source_section: Changing a hint gives a causal comparison
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed deterministic rule and its four evidence scores (-3, -2, -1, 1), with a hint worth two points. The other hint sizes, the 'far above zero' scores and the mixed-direction hint are the companion's own variations. No human or model data.
demonstrations.assumptions: A deterministic rule run on exactly the same cases both ways. The result covers these four cases and this hint; a stronger or weaker hint, another threshold or other scores can give a different result.
demonstrations.prediction: The hint adds two points. Predict the yes rate with and without it, and how many answers change.

state.direction: pushes toward yes in every case

reveal.text: The yes rate goes from one quarter to three quarters: Delta is 50 percentage points, and two answers changed. Switch the direction to 'first two toward yes, last two toward no': two answers still change, but the yes rate stays at one quarter and Delta is zero.

demonstrations.takeaway: Delta compares proportions on one scale, and an average can hide changes: two answers can flip in opposite directions and leave the yes rate where it was.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A causal claim about a cue needs the same cases run both ways. The average change and the count of changed cases answer different questions, so inspect the paired cases as well as the average.

sides.brain: Not applicable to a brain. The chapter's human studies change one thing and compare a report with the outcome; they are not a hint rule.
sides.machine: A specification: a rule we wrote, tested by setting an input ourselves. Real language models vary between runs, which the last demonstration shows.

demonstrations.explanation: The rule and the scores stay fixed and only the hint is set. Each case is answered twice, so we can see which answers changed. The yes rate under each setting gives Delta. Percentage points are used because the rate rises from one quarter to three quarters, a gap of half the scale, not a 50 percent rise.
demonstrations.check: For the chapter's four scores, what is the smallest hint size, in whole points, that changes any answer, and how many changes does it make?
demonstrations.answer: One point. Only the score of -1 reaches zero (-1 + 1 = 0, yes), so one answer changes and Delta is 25 percentage points. With two points the score of -2 changes as well.

controls.label: Direction of the hint
values: pushes toward yes in every case
toward yes in the first two, toward no in the last two
controls.default: pushes toward yes in every case

demonstrations.alt: Answers with and without a hint for four evidence scores with changes marked, and the change in yes rate against hint size.
demonstrations.symbols: Y: the answer: 1 for yes, 0 for no; H: the hint: 1 present, 0 absent; do(H = h): we set the hint ourselves to h; Delta: difference between the two proportions of yes, for these cases
demonstrations.application: A causal claim about a cue needs the same cases run both ways. The average change and the count of changed cases answer different questions, so inspect the paired cases as well as the average.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Hint's points: 2 · Direction of the hint: pushes toward yes in every case · Cases: the chapter's four scores
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: On the chapter's four scores the yes rate goes from 0.25 to 0.75 when the hint is set present, a change of 50 percentage points. 2 of the 4 answers changed, so the average and the count of changed answers are different things.

demonstrations.title: Does the report name the factor that changed the answer?
demonstrations.question: Among the answers the hint changed, what fraction of the reports name the hint?
equations: F_H=\frac{\#\{i:Y_i(1)\ne Y_i(0)\ \text{and report } i \text{ mentions } H\}}{\#\{i:Y_i(1)\ne Y_i(0)\}}

symbols_list.meaning: a case, here one of four evidence scores
the answer to case i with the hint present, and without it
a count
the share of changed decisions whose hint-present report mentions the hint

demonstrations.source_section: An explanation can miss a factor that changed an answer
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed rule and reports: with the hint at two points, score -1 is explained as tipped by the hint and score -2 as 'the available evidence supports yes', giving one of two. The report at score -3 (and at the unchanged score 1) is not fixed by the chapter; the companion sets it to 'does not name the hint'. The other hint sizes, report styles and the keyword checker are the companion's own variations; the chapter says a keyword search would miss other wording.
demonstrations.assumptions: Deterministic cases. 'Mention' is a deliberately narrow test and does not establish full faithfulness. The chapter fixes report wording only for scores -1 (names the hint) and -2 (does not). The report for score -3 is the companion's assumption (it does not name the hint); the same is true for the unchanged score 1.
demonstrations.prediction: With the chapter's report and a two-point hint, predict F_H. Then predict what happens if no answer changes.

reveal.text: Two answers change and one of the two reports names the hint, so F_H is one half. Set the hint to 0 points: no answer changes, so F_H is undefined rather than zero or one.

demonstrations.takeaway: F_H gives an explanation a chance to fail one specific check. When no decision changes the rate is undefined, and even a perfect rate would not establish full faithfulness.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A report can sound transparent and omit the cue that moved the answer, or name a cue that moved nothing. The test has to check the decision as well as the report.

sides.brain: In the stockings and choice blindness studies the reports were people's own and the researchers did not measure every influence on the original choice.
sides.machine: Turpin and colleagues and Chen and colleagues tested language models with biased prompts and hints and found reasons that did not name them. The chapter quotes noise-adjusted study scores of 25 percent for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39 percent for DeepSeek R1; those are model-based estimates, not this simple rate.

demonstrations.explanation: Compare each case's answer with and without the hint. Among cases where it changed, count the reports that name the hint. The bottom of the fraction is the number of changed answers, so with none the rate has no value. Words alone do not settle the causal question: a report can mention the hint and misstate how it was used, or name it where it changed nothing.
demonstrations.check: With the chapter's report and a hint of 3 points, three answers change. What is F_H?
demonstrations.answer: One third. Scores -3, -2 and -1 all change, and only the report at -1 names the hint. This takes the report at score -3 as not naming the hint, which is the companion's assumption, not the chapter's.
demonstrations.alt: A grid of four cases showing answer changed, report names the hint and keyword checker finds it, and acknowledgment rate against hint size.
demonstrations.symbols: i: a case, here one of four evidence scores; Y_i(1), Y_i(0): the answer to case i with the hint present, and without it; #: a count; F_H: the share of changed decisions whose hint-present report mentions the hint
demonstrations.application: A report can sound transparent and omit the cue that moved the answer, or name a cue that moved nothing. The test has to check the decision as well as the report.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Hint's points: 2 · Report style: the chapter's report
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A hint of 2 points changes 2 answers, and 1 of those 2 reports names it, so F_H = 0.5. A keyword checker finds 0.5. The report names the hint in 0 cases where it changed nothing, which F_H does not count.

demonstrations.title: How surprising are the position shares if position did not matter?
demonstrations.question: Shoppers favored items toward the right, 12 percent at the left to 40 percent at the right. What would equal chances give?

symbols_list.meaning: number of shoppers, 52
chance one position is chosen if all four positions are equally likely, one quarter
number of shoppers choosing that position
the count of shoppers choosing it

demonstrations.source_section: Position can affect a choice without appearing in the account
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's reported shares (12 to 40 percent across four positions, 52 shoppers, 80 recorded reasons with no mention of position). The counts are implied by rounding the shares and the chance calculation is the companion's own: the chapter and this book do not give the study's statistical analysis. Only the two extreme shares are given.
demonstrations.assumptions: An equal chance of one quarter for each position and independent shoppers; counts are the shares times 52, rounded. Shares other than 12 and 40 percent are hypothetical values for exploring the calculation; with 52 shoppers 20 and 30 percent cannot occur exactly (nearest counts 10 and 16). The chapter notes the authors did not know why the ordering appeared and considered that the order of inspection might matter.
demonstrations.prediction: At a 40 percent share, predict whether the chance of a count that far from 13 is below 5 in 100 for one position chosen in advance, and for the most extreme of four.

reveal.text: A 40 percent share is about 21 of 52, against 13 expected. The chance of a count that far out under equal chances is about 0.015 for a position chosen in advance, and at most about 0.061 when the most extreme of four is picked afterward, just above 0.05. This says the share is not easy to get by chance, not why it arose.

demonstrations.takeaway: On this simple calculation a count of about 21 out of 52 is unlikely under equal chances for one position chosen in advance, and borderline once the most extreme of four is picked afterward. It cannot say why, and it says nothing about any one shopper.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A group pattern can show that something other than the stated reasons shaped choices without saying which person was influenced. The reasons people gave and the pattern in their choices are different kinds of evidence.

sides.brain: Nisbett and Wilson's proposal, as the chapter states it, is that people sometimes infer the causes of their behavior from available information and their ideas about how choices work, which allows a report to be right. Nearly all shoppers denied position's influence when asked directly.
sides.machine: A language model faces a related test: shuffle the order of options and see whether the recommendation changes, while its explanation may discuss only the options.

demonstrations.explanation: If every position were equally likely, each would draw 13 of 52 shoppers on average, with some natural scatter. The count at the right is far above 13 and the count at the left is far below it. Because the position that looks extreme is picked after seeing the data, a more cautious comparison is with the most extreme of four, which is what the dashed line shows. That correction is the companion's own, not the study's analysis.
demonstrations.check: If the share at one position were 25 percent, what count is that, and how surprising is it under equal chances?
demonstrations.answer: 13 of 52, exactly the expected count, so a count at least this far from 13 has chance 1: it is not surprising at all.

controls.label: Position singled out
values: the most extreme of four positions

demonstrations.alt: Chance distribution of counts for one position among 52 shoppers with the observed count marked, and chance of each share on a log axis.
demonstrations.symbols: n: number of shoppers, 52; p: chance one position is chosen if all four positions are equally likely, one quarter; k: number of shoppers choosing that position; X: the count of shoppers choosing it
demonstrations.application: A group pattern can show that something other than the stated reasons shaped choices without saying which person was influenced. The reasons people gave and the pattern in their choices are different kinds of evidence.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Share choosing the position (percent): 40 · Position singled out: one position chosen in advance
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A 40 percent share is about 21 of 52 shoppers, against 13 expected if all four positions were equally likely. A count this far from 13 in either direction has chance 0.0153 for one position chosen in advance, and at most 0.0613 when the most extreme of four is picked afterward.

demonstrations.title: When the reasoning is part of the process, what does swapping a step show?
demonstrations.question: If a model writes an intermediate total and then uses it, what happens to the answer when the total is replaced?
equations: \text{final}=t\times 3,\quad t=12+5\ \text{originally; swap } t \text{ for another value}

symbols_list.meaning: the intermediate total written in the reasoning
the constructed problem's numbers: add 12 and 5, then multiply by 3
the last line of the answer

demonstrations.source_section: Written reasoning can also change the answer
demonstrations.provenance: A constructed arithmetic problem and three constructed procedures, the companion's own program. The chapter describes the swap test in words and cites Lanham and colleagues for interventions on generated reasoning, with effects that varied across tasks and tests; this program is not their experiment.
demonstrations.assumptions: Three procedures written to behave in three ways, so the outcome is known by construction. A real model's reasoning text and its numerical operations are not separate in this way.
demonstrations.prediction: Replace the written total 17 by 20 for each procedure. Predict which final answers change.

reveal.text: A procedure that reads the written total goes from 51 to 60. The other two stay at 51. Switch to 'recomputes from the inputs' and the swapped value is ignored: an unchanged answer cannot tell an unused step from a recovered one.

demonstrations.takeaway: A changed answer shows the later answer depended on the swapped step under that test. An unchanged answer does not show that written reasoning never matters.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: Whether the reasoning text is part of the process or only a report written afterward decides which test applies. Swapping a step is a way to find out which, for that step and that problem.

sides.machine: A language model generates text and then reads the text already generated, so intermediate text can become input to what comes next. The chapter treats written reasoning as something that can be experimentally changed, and as not automatically a complete account of what the model uses.
sides.brain: In the face study the explanation followed the choice, so it could not have caused it. The procedure decides which kind of explanation is being tested.

demonstrations.explanation: The reading procedure takes the written total as input to its last line, so the swap changes the answer. The recomputing procedure and the decide-first procedure get the answer from the inputs, so the swap leaves the answer alone. In the last case the text is a report written after the answer. In a real model an inserted mistake can also be an unusual input, and a model may recover by another route.
demonstrations.check: For the procedure that reads the written total, what final answer does a written total of 15 give, and what does that show?
demonstrations.answer: 15 x 3 = 45, different from 51, so the later answer depends on the written step under this test. It does not show how the original total was computed.

controls.label: Total placed in the written reasoning

demonstrations.alt: A small diagram of how inputs, the written total and the final line connect for the chosen procedure, and the final answer after each swap.
demonstrations.symbols: t: the intermediate total written in the reasoning; 12, 5, 3: the constructed problem's numbers: add 12 and 5, then multiply by 3; final: the last line of the answer
demonstrations.application: Whether the reasoning text is part of the process or only a report written afterward decides which test applies. Swapping a step is a way to find out which, for that step and that problem.
demonstrations.default_parameters: Total placed in the written reasoning: 20 · Procedure: reads the written total

worked_example.What the test shows: the later answer depends on the written step under this test

demonstrations.worked_interpretation: A procedure that reads the written total gives 51 before the swap and 60 after placing 20 where 17 was written. The answer changed, so the later answer depends on the written step under this test.

demonstrations.title: How many repeats does an order test need?
demonstrations.question: An assistant that varies from run to run compares two applications. How do we tell whether listing one first changes its recommendation?

symbols_list.meaning: how much better application A is on the assistant's scale (0.5 here)
order bias: points added to whichever application is listed first
run-to-run noise of the assistant's judgment (1 here)
the standard normal cumulative distribution

demonstrations.source_section: Written reasoning can also change the answer
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's constructed hiring assistant, described in words with no numbers: the chapter says these are possible tests, not results from an assistant. The gap, noise, biases and run counts are the companion's invented values and the runs are seeded simulations.
demonstrations.assumptions: A normal judgment noise and a fixed order bias, with one seeded run for each setting. The 95 percent range is a normal approximation with half a run added to each outcome, so it does not collapse to zero width when every run (or none) recommends A, and it is cut off at -1 and 1; it can still miss the exact value about 1 time in 20, and it is rough at 10 runs. A simulation is a computation, not a measurement of any assistant.
demonstrations.prediction: With a bias of 1 and only 10 runs per order, predict whether the estimated effect is reliably different from zero.

reveal.text: The exact effect of listing A first is 0.625, but with 10 runs per order the range around one seeded estimate (0.7, from 0.38 to 1, the top of the possible scale) is wide. Raise the runs to 160 or 640 and it narrows around the exact value.

demonstrations.takeaway: A deterministic assistant needs one swap to show order sensitivity. A noisy one needs repeated runs under each order, and the range around the estimate narrows only slowly with more runs.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A stable recommendation is also limited evidence: the order may have affected the reasoning without changing the final answer. The answer is only the outcome being measured.

sides.machine: The assistant is constructed. These are possible tests, not results from any assistant, and the order bias is set by us, not measured.
sides.brain: No brain study here has this design. Wilson and Nisbett's stockings study also found a position effect across a group, not for any one shopper.

demonstrations.explanation: With order bias, the chance of recommending A depends on where A is listed. The exact effect is the difference between the two chances. Each run gives only yes or no, so the effect is estimated from shares over repeated runs, with a range that depends on how many runs there are. The chapter also notes the evaluator should check whether the reported qualifications support the recommendation.
demonstrations.check: With no order bias, what is the exact effect, and could an estimate from 10 runs per order still be non-zero?
demonstrations.answer: Exactly zero, since both orders give the same chance (0.69). An estimate from 10 runs per order can still come out different from zero by chance, which is why the range is shown.
demonstrations.alt: Shares recommending application A when listed first and second with ranges and exact values, and the estimated order effect against bias.
demonstrations.symbols: g: how much better application A is on the assistant's scale (0.5 here); b: order bias: points added to whichever application is listed first; s: run-to-run noise of the assistant's judgment (1 here); Phi: the standard normal cumulative distribution
demonstrations.application: A stable recommendation is also limited evidence: the order may have affected the reasoning without changing the final answer. The answer is only the outcome being measured.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: With order bias 1 and 160 runs per order, the estimated effect of listing A first is 0.606 (range 0.525 to 0.687); the exact value is 0.625. One seeded run; a shorter series usually gives a wider range.

demonstrations.title: What does one changed answer tell us when runs vary?
demonstrations.question: If a model gives different answers on different runs, how often does one run per setting differ even when the hint has no effect?

symbols_list.meaning: chance of yes without and with the hint, for a case with score -1
run-to-run noise of the judgment
the true change in the chance of yes, p_1 - p_0

demonstrations.source_section: Changing a hint gives a causal comparison
demonstrations.provenance: The chapter's caution that one changed answer between two runs can reflect variation as well as the hint, made exact for a constructed noisy rule on the chapter's score of -1. The noise levels and hint sizes are the companion's, and the formula is exact, not simulated.
demonstrations.assumptions: Independent runs with normal judgment noise on a case with score -1. The chapter's own toy rule is deterministic, and this is the same rule with noise added.
demonstrations.prediction: Suppose the hint has no effect at all and noise is 1. Predict how often one run per setting would still show different answers.

reveal.text: With no hint effect, Delta is zero, yet one run per setting differs about 27 percent of the time (2 x 0.159 x 0.841). A single changed answer is not evidence of a hint effect.

demonstrations.takeaway: Repeated runs estimate how often each answer occurs. A single changed answer can come from variation alone, and the frequency of changes is not the same as the hint's effect.
demonstrations.why_it_matters: A model can mention a hint when its answer would have been the same without it, and a report can omit one that changes the frequency of an answer. State what outcome is compared.

sides.machine: A constructed noisy rule. Researchers repeat each condition, vary the order and report the uncertainty, as the chapter says; they should also inspect changes to answers other than the hinted one.

demonstrations.explanation: A noisy rule answers yes with some chance, and the hint raises that chance. One run under each setting gives one pair of answers. That pair can differ because of the hint or because of the noise. The chance that the pair differs is not the hint's effect, and it is positive even when the effect is zero.
demonstrations.check: With noise 1 and a hint of 2 points, the chances of yes are 0.159 and 0.841. What is Delta, and how often does one pair of runs differ?
demonstrations.alt: Chance of answering yes with and without a hint, and chance that one run per setting differs against hint size for three noise levels.
demonstrations.symbols: p_0, p_1: chance of yes without and with the hint, for a case with score -1; noise: run-to-run noise of the judgment; Delta: the true change in the chance of yes, p_1 - p_0
demonstrations.application: A model can mention a hint when its answer would have been the same without it, and a report can omit one that changes the frequency of an answer. State what outcome is compared.
demonstrations.worked_interpretation: The hint changes the chance of yes by 0, yet a single run per setting shows different answers 0.267 of the time. With no hint effect at all, a single pair of runs would still differ 0.267 of the time.
